title: Common Subordinating Conjunctions
goal: Choose common Norwegian subordinating conjunctions and recognize the dependent clauses they introduce.

objectives.statement: Choose common Norwegian subordinating conjunctions and recognize the dependent clauses they introduce.

spans.value: Maja and Jonas are preparing to spend Saturday at a cabin outside town. Maja calls Jonas on Friday evening because the weather forecast has changed.
Jeg tror at det blir mye regn i morgen.

blocks.translation: I think that there will be a lot of rain tomorrow.

spans.value: Skal vi avlyse turen fordi været blir dårlig?

blocks.translation: Should we cancel the trip because the weather is going to be bad?

spans.value: Nei, vi kan dra hvis veien er åpen.

blocks.translation: No, we can go if the road is open.

spans.value: Når skal vi bestemme oss?
Jeg sjekker værmeldingen før jeg legger meg, og jeg sender deg en melding når jeg våkner.

blocks.translation: I’ll check the weather forecast before I go to bed, and I’ll send you a message when I wake up.

spans.value: Bra. Jeg pakker regnjakka selv om jeg håper at vi ikke trenger den.

blocks.translation: Good. I’ll pack my rain jacket even though I hope that we won’t need it.

spans.value: Mens du pakker, kan jeg sjekke om butikken ved hytta er åpen.

blocks.translation: While you’re packing, I can check whether the shop near the cabin is open.

spans.value: The conversation is mainly about one decision: will Maja and Jonas go to the cabin? To discuss that decision, they connect ideas in several ways. Maja reports what she thinks, Jonas gives a reason, they state a condition, and they place actions in time.
The small connecting words make those relationships clear:

no.value: at

en.value: that

no.value: fordi

en.value: because

no.value: hvis

en.value: if

no.value: når

en.value: when

no.value: før

en.value: before

no.value: selv om

en.value: even though

no.value: mens

en.value: while

no.value: om

en.value: whether

spans.value: These words are subordinating conjunctions (subjunksjoner). A subordinating conjunction introduces a dependent clause (leddsetning): a group of words containing a subject and a verb that functions as part of a larger sentence.
In this sentence, the first part can stand as the main message:

no.value: Vi kan dra hvis veien er åpen.

en.value: We can go if the road is open.

spans.value: The dependent clause begins with hvis:

no.value: hvis veien er åpen

en.value: if the road is open

spans.value: It contains a subject, veien, and a verb, er. However, by itself it leaves an obvious question: what happens if the road is open? The main clause supplies that information.
Your task in this chapter is to choose a conjunction that expresses the intended relationship and to recognize the dependent clause that it introduces.

sections.title: Reporting a thought or statement with at

spans.value: Use at when one clause gives the content of a thought, belief, statement, or piece of information. It often corresponds to English that.

no.value: Maja tror at det blir regn.

en.value: Maja thinks that it will rain.

no.value: Jonas sier at han er klar.

en.value: Jonas says that he is ready.

no.value: Vi vet at veien er åpen.

en.value: We know that the road is open.

no.value: Jeg håper at butikken ikke er stengt.

en.value: I hope that the shop is not closed.

spans.value: In each example, the words after at tell us what someone thinks, says, knows, or hopes.
Compare the two parts:

no.value: Maja tror.

en.value: Maja thinks.

no.value: at det blir regn

en.value: that it will rain

spans.value: The first part is grammatically possible, but it does not tell us what Maja thinks. The at-clause provides the content.
A compact rule is:

statement.value: Use at to introduce the content of a thought, statement, belief, hope, or known fact.

spans.value: Do not choose at merely because English can sometimes omit that. Norwegian may also omit at in some informal contexts, but at is common, clear, and useful at this level.

no.value: Jeg tror at bussen kommer snart.

en.value: I think that the bus will arrive soon.

spans.value: The meaning is not a reason or a condition. The clause tells us what the speaker thinks.
Use fordi when the dependent clause explains why something happens or why someone makes a choice. It corresponds to because.

no.value: De vurderer å avlyse turen fordi været blir dårlig.

en.value: They are considering cancelling the trip because the weather is going to be bad.

no.value: Maja tar med støvler fordi det har regnet.

en.value: Maja is bringing boots because it has rained.

no.value: Jonas ringer fordi han har et spørsmål.

en.value: Jonas calls because he has a question.

no.value: Vi blir inne fordi det blåser mye.

en.value: We are staying inside because it is very windy.

spans.value: The fordi-clause answers a why-question.

no.value: Hvorfor tar Maja med støvler?

en.value: Why is Maja bringing boots?

no.value: Fordi det har regnet.

en.value: Because it has rained.

spans.value: In conversation, a fordi-clause can be used as a short answer when the missing main idea is already understood. In a full sentence, it belongs to a larger message:

no.value: Maja tar med støvler fordi det har regnet.

en.value: Maja is bringing boots because it has rained.

spans.value: A compact rule is:

statement.value: Use fordi when the dependent clause gives a reason.

spans.value: A common mistake is to choose fordi whenever two events are connected. The connection must specifically be one of cause or explanation.
Compare:

no.value: Vi drar hvis veien er åpen.

en.value: We will go if the road is open.

no.value: Vi drar fordi veien er åpen.

en.value: We are going because the road is open.

spans.value: The first sentence states a condition: the trip depends on the road being open. The second gives the open road as a reason for going.
Use hvis when an event or decision depends on a condition. It corresponds to if.

no.value: Vi drar hvis veien er åpen.

en.value: We will go if the road is open.

no.value: Jeg kjører hvis du er trøtt.

en.value: I’ll drive if you are tired.

no.value: Vi kan handle på veien hvis butikken ved hytta er stengt.

en.value: We can shop on the way if the shop near the cabin is closed.

no.value: Hvis det regner, blir vi inne.

en.value: If it rains, we will stay inside.

spans.value: The hvis-clause can come after or before the main clause. Its function remains the same: it gives the condition under which the main situation applies.

no.value: Jonas tar med ved hvis det blir kaldt.

en.value: Jonas will bring firewood if it gets cold.

no.value: Hvis det blir kaldt, tar Jonas med ved.

en.value: If it gets cold, Jonas will bring firewood.

spans.value: A compact rule is:

statement.value: Use hvis when the main event depends on a possible condition.

spans.value: Do not confuse a condition with a reason:

no.value: Jeg tar med mat hvis butikken er stengt.

en.value: I’ll bring food if the shop is closed.

spans.value: The speaker does not yet present the closure as a fact. It is a possibility that affects the plan.

no.value: Jeg tar med mat fordi butikken er stengt.

en.value: I’m bringing food because the shop is closed.

spans.value: Here, the closure is presented as the reason for the decision.

sections.title: Placing events in time with når, før, and mens

spans.value: Several common subordinating conjunctions tell us how two events relate in time.
Når: when
Use når to connect an event with a time or recurring situation.

no.value: Jeg sender deg en melding når jeg våkner.

en.value: I’ll send you a message when I wake up.

no.value: Når vi kommer fram, lager vi middag.

en.value: When we arrive, we will make dinner.

no.value: Jonas blir glad når han er på hytta.

en.value: Jonas is happy when he is at the cabin.

no.value: Vi spiller kort når det regner.

en.value: We play cards when it rains.

spans.value: In the dialogue, Maja has not woken up yet. Når introduces the future time at which she will send the message.
A compact rule is:

statement.value: Use når when one event occurs at the time another event occurs, especially in present, future, or repeated situations.

spans.value: A question beginning with når is not automatically a dependent clause:

no.value: Når skal vi bestemme oss?

en.value: When should we decide?

spans.value: This is a complete question. Compare it with:

no.value: Vi bestemmer oss når Maja har sjekket værmeldingen.

en.value: We will decide when Maja has checked the weather forecast.

spans.value: Here, når introduces the dependent clause:

no.value: når Maja har sjekket værmeldingen

en.value: when Maja has checked the weather forecast

spans.value: To recognize a dependent clause, look at its job in the sentence, not only at the word når. In the second example, the når-clause gives the time for the main decision.
Før: before
Use før when the event in the dependent clause happens later than the main event.

no.value: Maja sjekker værmeldingen før hun legger seg.

en.value: Maja checks the weather forecast before she goes to bed.

no.value: Vi kjøper mat før vi kjører til hytta.

en.value: We buy food before we drive to the cabin.

no.value: Jonas fyller bensin før han henter Maja.

en.value: Jonas gets petrol before he picks up Maja.

spans.value: In the first example, checking the forecast happens first. Going to bed happens afterward, although it appears inside the før-clause.
A compact rule is:

statement.value: Use før to mark the later event and show that the main event happens before it.

spans.value: Mens: while
Use mens when two situations happen during the same period.

no.value: Mens Jonas pakker, sjekker Maja butikken.

en.value: While Jonas is packing, Maja checks the shop.

no.value: Vi hører på radio mens vi kjører.

en.value: We listen to the radio while we drive.

no.value: Maja lager kaffe mens Jonas tenner i ovnen.

en.value: Maja makes coffee while Jonas lights the stove.

spans.value: A compact rule is:

statement.value: Use mens when two events or situations overlap in time.

spans.value: Compare these time relationships:

no.value: Jeg sjekker kartet før vi kjører.

en.value: I check the map before we drive.

no.value: Jeg sjekker kartet når vi stopper.

en.value: I check the map when we stop.

no.value: Jeg ser på kartet mens du kjører.

en.value: I look at the map while you drive.

spans.value: Før places one event before another. Når identifies the time at which something happens. Mens presents two actions as overlapping.

sections.title: Expressing an unexpected contrast with selv om

spans.value: Use selv om when the main situation is true despite something that might normally lead to a different result. It corresponds to even though or although.

no.value: Jonas pakker regnjakka selv om han håper på sol.

en.value: Jonas packs his rain jacket even though he hopes for sunshine.

no.value: De drar på tur selv om været er dårlig.

en.value: They go on the trip even though the weather is bad.

no.value: Maja er trøtt selv om hun har sovet lenge.

en.value: Maja is tired even though she has slept for a long time.

no.value: Selv om det regner, går de en liten tur.

en.value: Even though it is raining, they go for a short walk.

spans.value: The dependent clause introduces information that could create an expectation. The main clause shows that the expected result does not follow.
Bad weather might make us expect Maja and Jonas to stay home. Instead:

no.value: De drar selv om været er dårlig.

en.value: They go even though the weather is bad.

spans.value: A compact rule is:

statement.value: Use selv om when the main event happens despite the situation in the dependent clause.

spans.value: Do not use selv om for an ordinary reason:

no.value: De blir inne fordi det regner.

en.value: They stay inside because it is raining.

spans.value: The rain explains the decision.

no.value: De går ut selv om det regner.

en.value: They go outside even though it is raining.

spans.value: Going outside contrasts with the expectation created by the rain.
In the opening dialogue, Maja says:

no.value: Jeg kan sjekke om butikken ved hytta er åpen.

en.value: I can check whether the shop near the cabin is open.

spans.value: Here, om means whether. It introduces something that is uncertain and can be checked, asked, known, or discovered.

no.value: Jonas spør om veien er åpen.

en.value: Jonas asks whether the road is open.

no.value: Vi vet ikke om det blir regn.

en.value: We do not know whether it will rain.

no.value: Maja undersøker om bussen går på lørdager.

en.value: Maja checks whether the bus runs on Saturdays.

no.value: Jeg lurer på om hytta er varm.

en.value: I wonder whether the cabin is warm.

spans.value: A compact rule is:

statement.value: Use om to introduce an indirect yes-or-no question after expressions such as ask, know, check, or wonder.

spans.value: Compare at and om:

no.value: Jeg vet at butikken er åpen.

en.value: I know that the shop is open.

no.value: Jeg vet ikke om butikken er åpen.

en.value: I do not know whether the shop is open.

spans.value: With at, the speaker presents the information as known. With om, the question of whether the shop is open remains uncertain.
This distinction is about the relationship between the clauses:

items.value: at introduces content presented as a statement or fact;
om introduces an unresolved yes-or-no question.

spans.value: On Saturday morning, Maja checks the forecast again. The rain will arrive later than expected, and the road is open. She sends Jonas a message.
Jeg ser at veien er åpen.

blocks.translation: I can see that the road is open.

spans.value: Vi kan dra hvis du fortsatt har lyst.

blocks.translation: We can go if you still want to.

spans.value: Jeg vil dra selv om det kanskje blir regn i kveld.

blocks.translation: I want to go even though it may rain this evening.

spans.value: Kan du sjekke om vi trenger å ta med ved?

blocks.translation: Can you check whether we need to bring firewood?

spans.value: Jonas replies:
Ja. Jeg ringer eieren før jeg kjører hjemmefra.

blocks.translation: Yes. I’ll call the owner before I leave home.

spans.value: Mens jeg snakker med henne, kan jeg også spørre om butikken er åpen.

blocks.translation: While I’m speaking with her, I can also ask whether the shop is open.

spans.value: Jeg sender deg en melding når jeg vet mer.

blocks.translation: I’ll send you a message when I know more.

spans.value: The conjunctions let Maja and Jonas build one plan from several connected ideas. They report information with at, state a condition with hvis, accept an unexpected difficulty with selv om, investigate uncertainty with om, and organize actions with før, mens, and når.

sections.title: Cumulative transfer: planning a different day out

spans.value: Imagine that two friends, Amina and Henrik, are planning a Sunday bicycle ride. They need to consider rain, decide when to leave, check whether a café is open, and explain why they may change the route.
Without returning to the earlier explanations, recall which conjunction you would use to introduce:

items.value: an event that happens before another;

spans.value: Then write one connected Norwegian sentence about an everyday plan and underline the dependent clause. Choose a conjunction that matches the intended relationship, and underline the whole clause it introduces.

prompt.value: Choose the marking that shows all the subordinate clauses and how they connect to the main clause.

options.text: Amina sier [at] de sykler på søndag. Henrik tar med en regnjakke [fordi] værmeldingen melder regn. [Hvis] kafeen er åpen, stopper de [når] de kommer fram. De hører på radio [mens] de sykler, [selv om] det regner.

Amina sier [at de sykler på søndag] — det hun forteller; Henrik tar med en regnjakke [fordi værmeldingen melder regn] — grunn; [Hvis kafeen er åpen] — vilkår for stopp; de stopper [når de kommer fram] — tidspunkt for stopp; de hører på radio [mens de sykler] — samtidige handlinger; de hører på radio [selv om det regner] — uventet motsetning.
options.why: Alle leddsetningene er hele og knyttet til riktig funksjon.
